title: The Weedkiller in Your Food May Be Rewiring Your Brain Through Your Gut — and the 'Safe' Doses Aren't So Safe
excerpt: A wave of new research finds glyphosate — sprayed on wheat, oats, lentils, and most American crops — disrupts gut bacteria, alters brain chemistry, and triggers anxiety-like behavior at doses far below regulatory limits
body:
A growing body of research suggests that glyphosate — the active ingredient in Roundup and the most widely used herbicide on the planet — may be altering human behavior by disrupting the gut microbiome, even at doses regulators consider safe. The latest evidence, published June 30 in *Molecular Psychiatry*, adds to an increasingly uncomfortable picture for the 280 million pounds of the chemical sprayed on American crops each year.

The study, led by John F. Cryan at University College Cork — one of the world's foremost researchers on the gut-brain axis — found that glyphosate exposure disrupts behavior through changes in gut bacteria composition. The findings join a wave of peer-reviewed research linking the herbicide to anxiety-like behavior, impaired memory, and neuroinflammation through a mechanism scientists call the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

## What the Science Shows

The central finding across multiple recent studies is remarkably consistent: glyphosate, even at concentrations below regulatory safety thresholds, reduces populations of beneficial gut bacteria — particularly *Lactobacillus* species that play a critical role in producing serotonin, the neurotransmitter that regulates mood, sleep, and anxiety.

A study published in *Frontiers in Toxicology* found that rats given glyphosate at the dose the U.S. EPA considers safe for 16 weeks developed measurable increases in anxiety-like behavior and elevated threat responses. The behavioral changes corresponded with increased neural activity in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, a brain region directly implicated in anxiety disorders.

Perhaps most alarming is a study in *Environmental Science & Technology* that demonstrated the effect extends beyond mammals. Researchers found that glyphosate exposure at parts-per-billion concentrations — levels routinely found in tap water and processed foods — altered neurotransmitter levels in both the gut and brain, promoted anxiogenic behavior, and inhibited reproductive function.


![Molecular Psychiatry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/e/e3/Molecular_Psychiatry_%28cover%29.gif)



> **"The latest evidence, published June 30 in *Molecular Psychiatry*, adds to an increasingly uncomfortable picture for the 280 million pounds of the chemical sprayed on American crops each year."**



## The Dose Problem

The standard safety argument for glyphosate relies on the concept of an "acceptable daily intake" (ADI) — the amount regulators say a person can consume every day for a lifetime without harm. In the United States, that threshold is 1.75 mg/kg of body weight per day.

But a landmark study published in *Toxicological Sciences* found that mice exposed to glyphosate at just 0.01 mg/kg/day — 175 times below the EPA's safety limit and equivalent to typical dietary exposure for Americans — developed gut inflammation, metabolic dysfunction including insulin resistance, reduced GLP-1 levels, and behavioral deficits including impaired working memory. These effects persisted across two generations, suggesting the damage may be heritable.

The researchers found that glyphosate's metabolite, aminomethylphosphonic acid (AMPA), was present in brain tissue months after exposure ended, having crossed the blood-brain barrier — a finding with particular implications for populations already vulnerable to neuroinflammation, including those with early-stage Alzheimer's disease.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans navigating two food systems, the glyphosate question cuts both ways. The American food supply carries some of the highest glyphosate residue levels in the world. The herbicide is sprayed not just on genetically modified corn and soy — present in most processed foods — but is increasingly used as a pre-harvest desiccant on wheat, oats, and lentils, staples of the South Asian diet.


![University College Cork — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/County_Cork_-_University_College_Cork_-_20190125141016.jpg)


A 2023 U.S. Geological Survey analysis found glyphosate or its breakdown products in more than 70 percent of streams and rivers tested nationwide. The Environmental Working Group has detected measurable residues in popular oat-based cereals and snack bars.

India, meanwhile, is the world's largest producer of generic glyphosate and uses the chemical extensively on tea, cotton, and wheat — crops that supply both domestic and export markets. The Indian state of Kerala banned glyphosate in 2020 citing health concerns, but enforcement has been inconsistent, and the chemical remains widely available elsewhere in the country.

For NRIs who send food items to family in India, or who import Indian-grown spices, lentils, and teas, the question of residue levels in both directions is increasingly relevant.

## What You Can Do

The research doesn't call for panic, but it does suggest that the regulatory framework may be lagging behind the science. The studies point to several practical steps:

Choosing organic produce — particularly for wheat, oats, lentils, and soy — reduces glyphosate exposure significantly. Fermented foods like yogurt, idli, dosa batter, kimchi, and sauerkraut can help replenish *Lactobacillus* populations that glyphosate depletes. Prebiotic fiber from foods like garlic, onions, bananas, and whole grains supports the gut bacteria that appear most vulnerable to the herbicide.

The emerging science also raises questions about whether current regulatory safety thresholds — set decades ago based on acute toxicity studies — adequately account for the chronic, low-dose exposure that characterizes modern dietary contact with glyphosate.

As Cryan's team noted in their Molecular Psychiatry paper, the implications extend beyond individual health. If a ubiquitous agricultural chemical can subtly alter mood, cognition, and behavior at population scale through the gut microbiome, the public health calculus around herbicide regulation may need fundamental revision.

*Sources: Molecular Psychiatry (June 30, 2026); Frontiers in Toxicology; Environmental Science & Technology; Toxicological Sciences; Archives of Toxicology; U.S. Geological Survey; Environmental Working Group*
